claims.text: A nanocrystalline quinary WTaCrVHf refractory high-entropy alloy can exhibit high thermal stability and irradiation resistance.
The baseline WTaCrVHf alloy has a homogeneous microstructure.
The baseline alloy shows low defect generation and evolution under dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation.
The baseline alloy undergoes no detectable grain growth under the reported irradiation exposures.
A controlled 1–2 vol.% addition of nanoscale oxide particles such as Y2O3 should be introduced during processing.
The processing intervention will produce uniformly distributed nanoscale oxide precipitates in the alloy matrix.
Oxide nanoparticles will obstruct dislocation motion and provide dispersion strengthening.
Oxide nanoparticles will stabilize grain boundaries against thermal coarsening.
Oxide nanoparticles will stabilize grain boundaries against irradiation-induced coarsening.
Oxide addition will preserve the alloy's intrinsic resistance to irradiation-induced defects.
The oxide-treated alloy will improve yield strength by approximately 20–30% relative to the oxide-free baseline.
The oxide-treated alloy will improve hardness by approximately 20–30% relative to the oxide-free baseline.
The oxide-treated alloy will maintain grain stability under irradiation and high-temperature exposure.
The oxide-treated alloy will maintain low irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
The proposed benefit should hold at approximately 800–1000 °C under heavy-ion irradiation and helium implantation.
Nonuniform particle dispersion or excessive oxide volume fraction may cause clustering and embrittlement.
Particle clustering may cause thermal instability and offset the mechanical benefits.
The effectiveness of oxide dispersion may depend on oxide type and processing route.
